title: The ice realm and early warnings
teaches: Supercooled water and how ice makes rain, high ice clouds and the 22° halo, and reading an approaching warm front from first cirrus to nimbostratus

blocks.text: Anvil Peak, today we head all the way up to the high floor. High clouds look thin and delicate, and they give the earliest weather warnings you can get from a tower.

Climb high enough and the air stays below freezing even on a summer afternoon. Because the atmosphere cools by an average of about 6.5 °C for every kilometre of altitude, a mild 15 °C day in the valley reaches freezing (0 °C) a little over two kilometres up, drops to around −24 °C near the bottom of the high floor at six kilometres, and falls below −50 °C near the top of the troposphere. You might expect every cloud above the freezing level to be made of ice, yet most of them are still liquid water.

For liquid water to freeze, its jostling molecules have to lock into the regular six-sided lattice of an ice crystal. Just as water vapour needs a microscopic speck to condense onto, liquid water normally needs a solid template to start a crystal growing. In a lake or a puddle, plenty of suspended particles and rough surfaces trigger freezing right at 0 °C. A single cloud droplet, however, contains only the microscopic speck it originally condensed on. To trigger freezing, that speck needs an atomic spacing that closely matches the hexagonal geometry of ice so the first layer of water molecules can lock into place. Common condensation specks like sea salt, smoke, or soot have the wrong structure; only a few specific particles, such as certain mineral dusts, match the pattern of ice, amounting to perhaps one airborne particle in a million. Without an ice-forming nucleus, a tiny cloud droplet remains liquid well below 0 °C. Liquid water below the freezing point is called **supercooled**, and most clouds between 0 °C and −20 °C consist primarily of supercooled droplets. Only when the temperature drops below about −38 °C (rounded to −40 °C in the figure) do water molecules move slowly enough to lock into an ice crystal on their own, freezing every remaining droplet spontaneously.

blocks.caption: A mild summer day, from the valley floor to the top of the weather.

blocks.text: The atmosphere therefore divides into three temperature zones that shift up and down with the seasons: pure liquid droplets below the 0 °C freezing level, a mixed zone of supercooled droplets and scattered ice crystals between 0 °C and −40 °C, and pure ice crystals above the −40 °C level (around eight or nine kilometres up in summer). Although the high floor spans the upper part of the mixed zone as well as the pure-ice zone, high-floor clouds consist almost entirely of ice: near the top because droplets cannot stay liquid below −40 °C, and slightly lower down because any ice crystals that form rapidly consume the surrounding liquid droplets.

That mixed zone of supercooled droplets and ice crystals is where most of the world’s rain begins. In your first shift, you saw that air reaches its saturation limit when water molecules return to a liquid surface just as fast as they escape from it. In an ice crystal, each water molecule is held more tightly by its neighbours in the rigid lattice than it would be in liquid water at the same sub-freezing temperature, so molecules escape from an ice surface more slowly than from a supercooled droplet. Because molecules leave the ice more slowly, a lower concentration of surrounding water vapour is enough to replace them and keep the crystal in balance. At any temperature below 0 °C, the saturation vapour limit over ice is lower than the saturation limit over supercooled liquid water. At −12 °C, air that is just saturated with respect to liquid water contains about 13% more water vapour than is needed to saturate the air with respect to ice.

Now picture a single ice crystal floating among thousands of supercooled water droplets. At first, the surrounding air is kept right at the liquid saturation limit by the droplets, so molecules land on the droplets just as fast as they leave. For the ice crystal, however, that same vapour concentration is well above its saturation limit: water molecules land and lock onto the crystal much faster than they escape. As the crystal pulls water vapour out of the surrounding air, the vapour becomes slightly less crowded, dropping below the saturation limit of the liquid droplets. The droplets begin to evaporate, replenishing the water vapour in the air, which then deposits onto the growing ice crystal. Without ever touching the droplets, the ice crystal grows rapidly at their expense as water molecules evaporate from the liquid and freeze onto the ice.

blocks.caption: One ice crystal among supercooled cloud droplets.
blocks.task: Find a temperature where the crystal grows fast enough to fall.

blocks.text: As the temperature drops further below 0 °C, the percentage gap between the liquid and ice saturation limits widens, but very cold air holds so little water vapour overall that there are fewer molecules available to feed the crystal. The sweet spot where ice crystals grow fastest sits right between −10 °C and −15 °C. Within ten to twenty minutes, a crystal can grow heavy enough to start falling through the cloud. On its way down, it collides with supercooled droplets that freeze onto it on contact, or hooks together with other crystals to form snowflakes. When those snowflakes fall below the freezing level into warmer air, they melt into raindrops. Even in the middle of summer, most of the rain that falls on the forest around your tower starts out high in the cloud as snow. Weather radar shows this directly: just below the freezing level, rain clouds display a distinct bright band where large, wet, melting snowflakes reflect radar waves much more strongly than the smaller raindrops below.

Clouds that remain entirely warmer than freezing have to build raindrops exclusively through droplet collisions, which is a slow process. Clouds that reach high enough to tap into the −10 °C to −15 °C mixed zone can grow precipitation much more quickly through ice crystals. Either pathway still requires a deep cloud.

Up on the high floor, ice crystals form distinct clouds of their own. **Cirrus** consists of shafts of falling ice crystals. When crystals nucleate in a moist pocket near the top of the troposphere, they quickly grow to a tenth of a millimetre or more across (at least ten times the width of a typical liquid droplet) and fall at roughly half a metre to a metre per second. As the crystals descend into lower layers, they encounter air moving at different speeds. Because surface friction slows the wind near the ground while air high aloft flows unimpeded, wind speed usually changes with altitude, a variation known as **wind shear**. As falling crystals drop into slower-moving air below, they lag behind the faster-moving source pocket above, drawing the falling streak out into a long, curved trail.

blocks.caption: Ice crystals falling from a moist patch high up.
blocks.task: Add wind shear until the trails curl into hooks.

blocks.text: Those hooked, comma-shaped streaks are known as **mares’ tails**. The tufted head of the hook marks the pocket where new ice crystals are forming, while the long, trailing tail shows the crystals falling through wind shear and slowly sublimating back into water vapour in drier air below. Because ice crystals are much larger and far sparser than liquid cloud droplets (often fewer than one crystal for every thousand droplets in a low cloud), cirrus clouds look fibrous and silky, letting plenty of blue sky show through.

**Cirrocumulus** is the overturned, cellular layer of the high floor, appearing as tiny white grains or ripples arranged in regular rows like fish scales, a pattern sailors called a *mackerel sky*. Because the layer is very thin, the grains show no grey shading underneath. Cirrocumulus patches are usually short-lived, as the supercooled droplets that help start the ripples quickly freeze into cirrus streaks.

Because ice crystals have flat, angled faces rather than round surfaces like water droplets, they can refract sunlight into bright rings called halos. Light travels about 24% slower in ice than it does in air. When a beam of sunlight strikes an ice face at an angle, the side of the beam that enters the ice first slows down first while the other side is still travelling at full speed in air. That speed difference pivots the beam toward the slower side, just as a row of marching musicians turns when the people on one end shorten their stride. When the beam exits the crystal back into air, the edge that emerges first speeds up first, bending the light a second time.

Many high-altitude ice crystals grow as tiny hexagonal columns or plates, shaped like short lengths of a six-sided pencil. If a ray of light enters one side face and strikes the adjacent face (which meets it at a 120° angle), it hits that interior surface at too shallow an angle to escape and reflects back inside the crystal. If the ray instead passes through the crystal and exits through an alternate side face (skipping one face between entry and exit), those two faces slant toward each other at a 60° angle. The ice crystal then acts, optically, like a 60° prism.

blocks.caption: Sunlight through one hexagonal ice crystal.
blocks.task: Turn the crystal until the light is bent the least.

blocks.text: The deflection angle is the angle between the ray’s original path from the sun and the direction it travels after leaving the crystal. No matter how you rotate a hexagonal crystal, a ray passing through its 60° prism faces is deflected by **at least 22°** (21.8° for yellow light, as shown in the figure). Even more importantly, right around that minimum angle, rotating the crystal by several degrees barely changes the outgoing angle at all, just as the slope of the ground is nearly flat right at the bottom of a valley. When millions of crystals are tumbling at random angles in the sky, a wide range of crystal orientations all deflect sunlight out at nearly 22°, whereas larger deflection angles receive light from far fewer orientations. As a result, refracted sunlight concentrates strongly right along the 22° minimum angle.

When a high cloud veil fills the sky with millions of randomly oriented hexagonal crystals, those crystals deflect sunlight in all directions by 22° or more, with the strongest concentration right at 22°. Looking up toward the sun from the ground, the rays deflected toward your eye arrive from a bright circle surrounding the sun at an angular radius of 22°.

blocks.caption: Sunlight through a sky of randomly turned crystals.
blocks.task: Add crystals until the ring appears.

blocks.text: That bright ring is the **22° halo**. The sky just inside the ring looks noticeably darker than the sky outside it because no ray passing through a 60° ice prism can be bent by less than the minimum angle, leaving a sharp inner boundary. That inner edge is tinted faintly red: ice slows red light slightly less than blue light, so red light has a minimum deflection of about 21.5° while blue light bends by at least 22.4°. Red light therefore forms the innermost rim of the circle, while the other colours overlap further out and blend back into white. On the sky, a 22° radius is quite large: if you stretch your arm out straight and spread your fingers wide, the distance from the sun to the halo spans roughly from the tip of your thumb to the tip of your little finger.

Because only hexagonal ice crystals produce a 22° ring, and forming a complete circle requires crystals distributed evenly across the sky, a full halo is the signature of **cirrostratus**. Cirrostratus is a thin, milky veil of ice crystals covering the sky, translucent enough that the sun’s outline stays sharp and objects on the ground still cast clear shadows. Whether a cirrostratus halo is harmless or a warning depends on how the sky changes over the next few hours.

parts.title: A warm front, from far off

blocks.text: Pay close attention to this sequence, Anvil Peak. Watching how high clouds evolve over the course of a day is one of the best ways to spot an incoming storm system.

Across the mid-latitudes, huge air masses hundreds of kilometres wide move across the continent, some carrying warm, moist air from lower latitudes and others bringing cool, denser air from closer to the poles. When an advancing mass of warm air overtakes a retreating wedge of cold air, the boundary between them is called a **warm front**. Because the warm air is less dense than the cold air ahead of it, it cannot easily shove the heavy cold air out of the way; instead, it glides up and over the cold wedge along a very gentle slope, rising only about one kilometre vertically for every hundred kilometres horizontally.

As the warm, moist air glides up that gradual ramp, it expands and cools across a region hundreds of kilometres wide, forming broad cloud sheets at every level along the slope. Because the frontal slope is roughly 1 in 100, the top of the ramp at an altitude of ten kilometres sits nearly a thousand kilometres ahead of the surface boundary where the front touches the ground. To an observer on the tower, an approaching warm front arrives backwards from top to bottom: you see its highest ice clouds first, followed by progressively lower and thicker layers as the wedge of cold air retreats. Since a typical warm front advances at around 25 kilometres per hour, those first high cirrus streaks can appear overhead a day and a half before the surface front arrives.

blocks.caption: A warm front, moving towards the lookout at about 25 km/h.
blocks.task: Let the front come in until rain is about to arrive.

blocks.text: This top-down progression gives you a reliable timeline from the lookout tower: detached **cirrus** hooks invading from one side of the horizon, thickening into a milky **cirrostratus** veil with a 22° halo, lowering and greying into **altostratus** that dims the sun into a frosted disc and washes out the halo, and finally deepening into an overcast rain deck. Rain begins well before the surface front reaches you, as soon as the cloud deck overhead grows deep enough to span from the ice-growth zone down to the lower sky, typically across the last two or three hundred kilometres ahead of the surface boundary. From the time you first spot a halo in thickening cirrostratus, steady rain usually arrives within **12 to 24 hours**; once altostratus has hidden the sharp disc of the sun, rain is only a few hours away.

Moonlight refracts through cirrostratus at the exact same 22° angle at night, which is where the old saying 'ring around the moon, rain soon' comes from. Sometimes a high veil passes by without a full front behind it, but when the veil keeps thickening, the old rhyme holds up well.

The final, deepest cloud along the warm front is **nimbostratus**, a dark, featureless grey layer several kilometres thick that produces hours of continuous rain or snow. It combines broad frontal lifting, which gives it the horizontal extent of a sheet, with great vertical depth stretching from the low sky right up through the freezing level into the mixed ice-and-water zone, where snow crystals grow rapidly and melt on the way down into steady rain.

In the naming system, *nimbo-* indicates a rain-bearing cloud rather than a specific altitude floor. The International Cloud Atlas classifies nimbostratus as a middle-floor cloud because its main body develops in the middle levels, though it regularly thickens downward into the low floor. As rain falls out of the base into the air below, some of the drops evaporate, both cooling the sub-cloud air and adding water vapour to it. Before long, pockets of air beneath the main deck reach their dew point and condense into ragged, fast-moving shreds of low cloud known as **scud** (or pannus), making the dark base appear to sag toward the ridges.

blocks.caption: The sun behind the front’s layer of cloud.
blocks.task: Thicken the layer until the sun is gone entirely.

blocks.text: From the tower, the quickest way to tell when thickening altostratus has turned into nimbostratus is to look for the sun: through altostratus you can still make out its pale disc, whereas nimbostratus is so deep and dense that it blots out the sun’s position completely. You can also distinguish nimbostratus from a dark layer of low stratocumulus by its lack of structure. Stratocumulus has a clear underside with distinct lumps, rolls, and contrast between lighter and darker patches; nimbostratus has a uniform, diffuse grey base that looks blurred and indistinct behind curtains of falling rain.
Radio check, Anvil Peak. First call in the cloud types from the lookouts’ photos, and then tell me what these changing skies mean for the crews.

blocks.caption: Photos from the other lookouts. Call in each cloud by name.
The sky over a few hours, as the other lookouts logged it. What is it up to?

items.question: Mares’ tails thickened into a milky veil with a halo; now the halo has faded and the sun is just a dim disc. When should the crews expect rain?
options: No rain expected; this is fair weather
items.why: A progression from cirrus to cirrostratus and then to thickening altostratus marks an approaching warm front. Rain usually arrives within 12 to 24 hours of the first halo, and within just a few hours once altostratus dims the sun.

items.question: A few wispy streaks of cirrus have drifted across the blue sky all day without spreading or thickening. What is the forecast?
options: A warm front arriving within hours
items.why: Isolated cirrus wisps on their own simply show moist pockets in the upper troposphere. Only when cirrus spreads and thickens into a continuous cirrostratus veil does it warn of an approaching warm front.

items.question: A grey middle-level sheet has thickened until the sun is completely hidden and the base looks dark and blurred. What should the crews expect?
options: A brief passing shower, followed by sun
The layer will burn off by midday
items.why: A deep, featureless grey deck that completely hides the sun and blurs into falling precipitation is nimbostratus, which brings hours of steady frontal rain.

items.question: A milky veil of cirrostratus produces a bright ring around the sun. Roughly how wide is the radius of that ring?
items.why: Light passing through the 60° prism faces of hexagonal ice crystals bends by a minimum of 22°, which matches the span from thumb to little finger on an outstretched hand.

learned: Pure cloud droplets lack ice-forming nuclei and stay liquid well below 0 °C (supercooled), only freezing spontaneously below about −38 °C; high-floor clouds consist almost entirely of ice crystals.

Because water molecules escape more slowly from ice than from supercooled liquid water, the saturation vapour limit over ice is lower; ice crystals in a mixed cloud grow rapidly by drawing in vapour as surrounding droplets evaporate, meaning most rain starts high up as snow.
Cirrus hooks (mares’ tails) are trails of falling ice crystals curved by wind shear as wind speed changes with altitude.

Sunlight passing through the 60° prism faces of hexagonal ice crystals bends by a minimum of 22°, concentrating light into a 22° halo (roughly a spread hand-span in radius) when a cirrostratus veil covers the sky.

Along an approaching warm front, warm air glides up over a retreating wedge of cold air, producing a top-down sequence of clouds: cirrus, cirrostratus with a halo, altostratus, and finally deep nimbostratus with steady rain arriving 12 to 24 hours after the halo.

ice.title: The ice realm
ice.text: Because freezing requires a rare type of microscopic particle whose atomic spacing matches the hexagonal lattice of ice, cloud droplets remain liquid well below 0 °C as supercooled water, freezing spontaneously only below about −38 °C. Between 0 °C and −38 °C, clouds often contain a mix of supercooled droplets and ice crystals, while high-floor clouds consist almost entirely of ice. Because ice crystals are larger and far sparser than droplets, high clouds look thin and fibrous, trail into falling streaks, and refract sunlight into halos.

ice-rain.title: How ice makes rain
ice-rain.text: At sub-freezing temperatures, the saturation vapour limit over ice is lower than over supercooled water because molecules are bound more tightly in the ice crystal. In a mixed cloud, ice crystals grow rapidly as water vapour deposits onto the ice while surrounding supercooled droplets evaporate to replenish the vapour, working fastest between −10 °C and −15 °C. Once heavy enough, the crystals fall, collect more droplets or clump into snowflakes, and melt in warmer air below to reach the ground as rain.

cirrus.title: Cirrus
cirrus.text: Detached, fibrous white filaments and hooked streaks (mares’ tails) on the high floor, formed by ice crystals falling through wind shear and sublimating in drier air below. Isolated cirrus indicates fair weather, whereas cirrus thickening and spreading across the sky warns of an approaching front.

cirrostratus.title: Cirrostratus
cirrostratus.text: A thin, whitish veil of ice crystals covering much or all of the high sky. The sun’s outline remains clear, ground shadows remain visible, and the layer frequently produces a 22° halo around the sun or moon. Thickening cirrostratus ahead of a warm front typically signals steady rain within 12 to 24 hours.

cirrocumulus.title: Cirrocumulus
cirrocumulus.text: A thin high-altitude layer of tiny white grains or ripples without grey shading (a mackerel sky), where each element is smaller than a little-finger nail held at arm’s length. Cirrocumulus patches are brief and transitional, sometimes appearing ahead of an approaching weather system.

halo.title: The 22° halo
halo.text: Sunlight entering one side face of a hexagonal ice crystal and exiting two faces around passes through a 60° prism, bending by at least 22°. Millions of randomly tumbling crystals in cirrostratus concentrate refracted light right near that minimum angle, forming a bright ring of 22° radius (about a spread hand-span at arm’s length) around the sun or moon with a faintly reddish inner rim.

warm-front.title: A warm front coming
warm-front.text: At a warm front, advancing warm air glides up over a retreating wedge of denser cold air along a gentle slope of roughly 1 in 100, forming layered clouds that extend up to a thousand kilometres ahead of the surface boundary. An observer sees the highest clouds first: cirrus hooks, then a cirrostratus veil with a 22° halo, then lowering altostratus that dims the sun, and finally deep nimbostratus bringing steady rain 12 to 24 hours after the halo.

nimbostratus.title: Nimbostratus
nimbostratus.text: A dark, featureless grey cloud deck several kilometres deep that completely blots out the sun and produces hours of continuous rain or snow. Its upper reaches extend into the sub-freezing mixed zone where ice crystals rapidly generate precipitation, while evaporating rain below its base often forms ragged shreds of low scud.
